Surreptitiously means doing something in a secret, careful, sneaky way — specifically because you know it is not allowed, or you know that others would disapprove or stop you if they noticed.

You are hiding what you are doing on purpose, and you are being careful about it.

There are really two things packed into this word at the same time:

  1. Secrecy — others do not know what you are doing.
  2. Awareness of wrongdoing — you know (or strongly sense) that the action is forbidden, disapproved of, or at least frowned upon. That is why you are hiding it.

This combination is what makes the word special. It is not just doing something in secret. It has a slightly guilty, sneaky quality to it. The person doing the action is conscious that they are doing something they probably should not be doing.

• During the exam, she surreptitiously glanced at her neighbor's paper.

(She was cheating — something not allowed — and she was being careful not to let the teacher see.)

  • He surreptitiously slipped a note to his friend during the board meeting.

(Passing notes during a formal meeting is not appropriate, so he did it quietly and carefully.)

  • The child surreptitiously grabbed a cookie from the jar while his mother had her back turned.

(He knew he was not supposed to have a cookie before dinner, so he was sneaky about it.)

  • She surreptitiously checked her phone during the movie.

(Using your phone in a cinema is considered rude, so she tried to do it without anyone noticing.)

Notice the common thread: in every case, the person knows they are doing something they are not supposed to, and they are being deliberate and careful about not getting caught.
How it differs from similar words

This is where many learners get confused, so it is worth spending time here.

Secretly is a neutral, everyday word. It simply means "without others knowing." There is no suggestion of sneakiness or guilt. "She secretly admired his courage" — there is no wrongdoing here, just a private feeling. You would not say "surreptitiously" in this case, because she is not hiding something forbidden.

Stealthily focuses mainly on physical quietness and careful movement — like a cat creeping toward a bird. It is about how you move your body. It does not necessarily carry any moral weight or imply wrongdoing. A soldier moving stealthily through a forest is being quiet, not necessarily guilty.

Covertly is a more formal, professional word used mainly in military, government, or intelligence contexts. "The agents covertly gathered information." It is about operational secrecy. Personal guilt or sneakiness is not really the focus.

Discreetly is almost the opposite in feel, even though it involves not drawing attention. When you do something discreetly, you are being tactful and careful to avoid causing embarrassment or awkwardness — and this is generally seen as a good quality. "She discreetly reminded him that his microphone was still on." There is no wrongdoing at all; it is considered considerate behavior.

Furtively is the word most similar to surreptitiously, and they are often used interchangeably. The subtle difference: furtively tends to emphasize the nervous, anxious feeling of someone afraid of being caught — think of darting eyes, quick glances over the shoulder, jumpy behavior. Surreptitiously focuses more on the deliberate, careful act of concealing what you are doing. In practice, the difference is small, but if you picture someone stealing something, their behavior (nervous, shifty) is furtive, while their action (carefully sliding it under their coat) is surreptitious.

Whenever you are unsure whether to use this word, ask yourself:

Is this person doing something they know they should not, or that others would object to — and are they carefully and deliberately hiding it?

If the answer is yes, surreptitiously is likely the right word.

This is a formal, sophisticated word. You will encounter it most often in writing — novels, journalism, essays, formal reports. In casual everyday speech, people would more naturally say "sneakily", "on the sly", or "behind someone's back."

If you use "surreptitiously" in a conversation or piece of writing, it signals careful, educated use of language. It is never wrong to use it; it just sounds more formal than its casual equivalents.

Can surreptitiously be used even when there is no real wrongdoing? Occasionally, yes — but even then, the feeling of wanting to hide something from others remains. For example: "She surreptitiously studied his face, trying to read his expression." She is not doing anything wrong, but she does not want him to notice that she is watching him carefully. That slight self-conscious concealment is what keeps the word appropriate here.

The core of the word is always: deliberate, careful concealment of an action, driven by the awareness that it would not be approved of if noticed.
